rows.question: What kinds of old photos do users struggle to retrieve?
rows.restated: What kinds of old photos do users struggle to retrieve?
rows.text:
**People struggle to retrieve a wide range of old photos, but about a third of the cases where someone only vaguely remembered the image still ended with them finding it and about a quarter ended when their search returned no matching results.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]

The posts show examples across family memories ("old baby photos", the post says), documents/screenshots ("I need old screenshot picc", the post says; "driver's license", the post says), and casual snapshots (finding old relationship screenshots, the post says), so the trouble affects memory photos and information photos alike. [[story|e7e4eb6a20b124405577ba1cd0fa0775014739c9:0]][[story|313e52d4d7afb19798f4bb12be3491ecf5803425:0]][[story|b526179286c2b3c9db1c198db44e50543ed2f275:0]][[story|765749899f7fa8a7f4c8527cc2337029e134b9ce:0]]

My read is that the pattern is simple: when people have a half-memory, either they can translate it into a query and spot the result (about a third), or they do translate it but the photo isn't in the results (about a quarter); smaller numbers report the photo was already gone or they never used search. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:_all]]

Unfortunately the cases are too few to compare types directly, and photos kept for information appear in only 21 cases so I give counts not shares: 8 of those were already gone, six were found, four lacked enough memory to search, and three returned no result. [[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]]

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed or remembered when they searched?*

rows.question: What information do people actually remember about a photo?
rows.restated: What information do people actually remember about a photo?
rows.gap: two AI readers went through the stories separately and agreed too rarely on what they actually remember about the photo to rely on it
rows.text:
**People most often remember what’s in the photo: about two in five of the 115 cases say the poster remembered the photo’s content.** The posts say they recalled the main subject or visible things in 47 of the 115 cases (the post says they remembered what was in it) and the tagged lines list more specific content memories (main subject 29, objects 9, visible text 4, activity 5) [[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:what:core]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.1=what:main_subject@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.1=what:objects@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.1=what:visible_text@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.1=what:activity@photo_class:_all]]. 

I’m afraid the posts can’t settle everything: two AI readers disagreed too often about what people actually remembered, so we can’t trust finer splits beyond the counts given [[analysis_reliability|q:2.1]][[analysis_method_flags|no_gold_standard]]. My read is that when people can name the subject (a person, object or scene) they report it most, and less often remember time, place or relationship — the evidence shows remembering when in about one in five cases and who in about one in eight cases [[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:when:core]][[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:who:core]]. This suggests improving search for short content descriptions would match the largest group; making date/place cues easier helps a smaller but real group.

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed when describing the photo?*

rows.question: What information have people forgotten about the photo they want?
rows.restated: What kinds of information (what, when, who, where, event, etc.) did people say they had forgotten about the photo they were trying to find?
rows.text:
**People looking for a vaguely remembered photo most often have forgotten when it was taken — about one in eight cases say so.** [[analysis_derived|cue_forgotten:when:core]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.4=date_or_year@photo_class:_all]]

The posts show smaller numbers for other missing details: about one in twenty say they’d forgotten where it was taken, and only a handful mention not knowing whether the item was a screenshot or which app/account it came from. [[analysis_derived|cue_forgotten:where:core]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.4=exact_place_or_venue_name@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.4=photo_video_or_screenshot@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.4=which_app_or_account@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_derived|cue_forgotten:source:core]]

My read is that timing is the single clearest gap: many people can recall who or what is in the image but not the date, so they reach for time-based cues and fail when those are absent. [[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:what:core]][[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:when:core]][[analysis_derived|cue_forgotten:when:core]] This suggests improving ways to search by fuzzy time or to surface likely-date anchors could help. A caveat — only 99 of the 115 cases say anything about what was forgotten, so treat the exact shares cautiously. [[analysis_coverage|2.4]][[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]]

*Want to see the exact phrases people used when they said they’d forgotten the date or place?*

rows.question: How do users formulate searches when their memory is incomplete?
rows.restated: How do users formulate searches when their memory is incomplete?
rows.text:
**When people only half-remember a photo, about a quarter first type a single word into search, while only a handful type a full sentence or a name.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=full_natural_description@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=named_entity@photo_class:_all]]

The posts that say what was typed show single words like "vomit", "bicycle", "passport", "dog", "tatoo" and short keywords such as "photo frames" or "driver's license" — the post says they began with those words and then looked at results. [[story|88a83897e2c872e72ac85967d7fc5c158d43bbb0:0]][[story|790de55c9d650cb50647f97841544a0c5b1b7275:0]][[story|4bc6fae93ac441d7708072e0871976ae3562b9a6:0]][[story|c0d1dafa88ec6dba2c4741ebdda4c7a72aed14ac:0]][[story|c06874c9c9acadf8038072c41b2d0d2c08c2bc10:0]][[story|765749899f7fa8a7f4c8527cc2337029e134b9ce:0]][[story|aa1520f4fbb8f25b2e1435cc95c2f9fd8d6616fe:0]][[story|247694a905c13ced6a041728c4685f9c02dcbd78:0]] My read is that when memory is thin people try a short, focal cue first because it’s quick and feels most likely to match a visual label.

This matters because the study also shows that in about a quarter of cases the first thing that went wrong was searching with what they remembered but the photo wasn't in the results, so improving how short queries are handled would reach a large group. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:_all]]

I'm afraid the posts can't settle why specific short queries failed (we can't see internal search behaviour) or how often people tried more than one phrasing before giving up. [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=named_entity@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]]

*Want to see the exact short phrases people typed first?*

rows.question: Does Google Photos fail to understand the clues people give it?
rows.restated: Does Google Photos fail to understand the clues people give it?
dropped: I'm afraid the posts cannot settle why search failed internally (we cannot see system logs) or how often this happens across all users; the counts are only for these public cases.
rows.text:
**Yes — in roughly a quarter of cases about a vaguely remembered photo, people say they searched with the clue they had but the photo did not appear in the results.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]

The evidence — the team read public posts and traced each search attempt; in 31 of 115 cases the first failure was that the person searched with what they remembered but the photo wasn't in the results. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]] A likely reason is that short, partial clues (single words or brief phrases such as "screenshot picc", "wearing green clothes kit of football", or "dog in pool") are hard to match reliably from a user’s memory to the photos' searchable metadata or automatic labels — so search returns nothing or irrelevant images instead. [[story|313e52d4d7afb19798f4bb12be3491ecf5803425:0]][[story|912c6cc3068a194559168f5b66e2dbc5bc867dc8:0]][[story|c06874c9c9acadf8038072c41b2d0d2c08c2bc10:0]][[story|3ba2ad97300ec1206044dc3deed79e0240a13297:1]]

What that implies — improving how the product handles brief, imprecise queries — better interpretation of short phrases, richer query expansion, or offering guided suggestions when results are empty — would reach the largest single group of failures in these cases. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed when search first failed?*

rows.question: What is Google Photos' annual revenue?
rows.restated: What is Google Photos' annual revenue?
rows.gap: these are public stories, not usage data: no rate of success or failure, and no count of users, can be produced from them
rows.text:
I'm afraid the posts we read are public user accounts about finding photos in Google Photos; they contain no financial or corporate revenue data, so they cannot answer Google Photos' annual revenue. The study is about people hunting for a particular photo and where that search process breaks down, not about business finances.

*Would you like figures on what people typed when a search failed instead?*

rows.question: How many people use Ask Photos every month?
rows.restated: How many people use Ask Photos every month?
rows.gap: these are public stories, not usage data: no rate of success or failure, and no count of users, can be produced from them
rows.text:
I'm afraid the study can't answer that — it examined public posts about hunting for single photos, not any usage or traffic data, so it cannot give monthly user counts. The study is about where search fails people with a half-memory, not how many people use Ask Photos.

*Would you like to see what the posts say about what people typed when search failed?*

rows.question: What is the success rate for searches from vague memories?
rows.restated: What fraction of searches that start from a vague memory successfully find the photo?
rows.gap: these are public stories, not usage data: no rate of success or failure, and no count of users, can be produced from them
rows.text:
I'm afraid the study can't answer that: it used public posts about particular hunts, not usage logs, so it cannot produce a success or failure rate for searches from vague memories. The study instead analyses where along the hunting path people say the attempt broke down and what kinds of memory or interaction problems appear.

*Would you like to see the counts for where people said the hunt first went wrong?*

rows.question: Do Android users struggle to find photos more than iPhone users?
rows.restated: Do Android users struggle to find photos more than iPhone users?
rows.gap: the posts do not reliably say which phone people use, so there is no Android vs iPhone split
dropped: The posts mostly do not say which phone people used, so no Android vs iPhone split is possible .
rows.text:
**I’m afraid the posts cannot settle whether Android users struggle more than iPhone users.**

That said, the study does tell us where searches went wrong for the 115 cases about vaguely remembered photos: what people remembered, how they searched, and what search showed, so we can compare problems across those dimensions but not by phone [[analysis_funnel|stories:core]][[analysis_coverage|2.1]][[analysis_coverage|4.1]][[analysis_coverage|5.6]]. My read is that to answer your question we would need phone type recorded in the cases; the public posts simply don’t provide that detail [[analysis_method_flags|missing_cuts]].

If you want a usable comparison, we can pull from the 314 posts and count which mention phone type and then compare their search paths—but the current evidence can’t do that reliably.

*Want me to gather the posts that do name a phone and show which steps they describe?*

rows.question: Has search got worse since Ask Photos launched?
rows.restated: Is Google Photos search worse now than it was before Ask Photos launched?
rows.gap: the stories were not compared across time, so there is no before-and-after
rows.text:
**No — the posts cannot show whether search got worse after Ask Photos launched; the data contain no valid before‑and‑after comparison.** [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]]

Having said that, the study can still say what people reported struggling with after they tried to find a vaguely remembered photo, and where the evidence points for product fixes. The cases about vague memories (115 people) most often report trouble turning their memory into words and then failing to see the photo in results: 192 of 331 cases say what they remembered, but only 61 of 290 say whether search understood what they typed, and only 46 of 331 say what search showed them — so the record is thin about exact search behaviour and outcomes. [[analysis_funnel|stories:core]][[analysis_coverage|2.1]][[analysis_coverage|5.1]][[analysis_coverage|5.6]]

My read is that improving short-query reading and result surfacing would help the largest visible group because many posts describe typing a natural clue and then not finding the photo, or finding irrelevant clusters instead (examples: “it found photos of my cats instead of me with beard journey”; “it returned way too many images of my shop”; “after scrolling enough it was right there”). [[story|3ba2ad97300ec1206044dc3deed79e0240a13297:1]][[story|0ef3821f2d59998617a4b53f428fd49c9a22d2ff:0]][[story|1e8838fe6fe7c3028b1b5caf63177262024a2878:1]]

I'm afraid the posts can't settle whether any change after Ask Photos made this better or worse. [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]]

*Want to see what people actually typed first?*

rows.question: Is Apple Photos search better than Google Photos search at finding old photos?
rows.restated: Is Apple Photos search better than Google Photos search at finding old photos?
rows.gap: the stories do not compare how well other photo apps search
rows.text:
**I’m afraid the posts cannot settle whether Apple Photos search is better than Google Photos search — the data are only public posts about finding photos and do not compare apps.** [[analysis_method_flags|missing_cuts]][[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]]

That said, the study does tell us, for people who posted about a vaguely remembered photo in Google Photos, where searches commonly faltered and what might help. The most informative pattern is that about two in five of those vague-photo cases came from X (Twitter) and about a quarter came from YouTube comments, so the sample skews to those venues. [[analysis_crosstab|core.source=x@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.source=youtube@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|collected]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

Reading the path people described shows search failures fall into a few visible problems: many people reported what search showed them (when they said anything) as irrelevant or overwhelmingly broad — for example, “it returned way too many images of my shop” and “it found photos of my cats instead of me with beard journey.” [[analysis_coverage|5.6]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:5.6=irrelevant_results@photo_class:_all]][[story|0ef3821f2d59998617a4b53f428fd49c9a22d2ff:0]][[story|3ba2ad97300ec1206044dc3deed79e0240a13297:1]] My read is that improving how short or single-word queries are interpreted would help the largest visible group, because about a quarter of cases that report what they typed first say they began with a single word. [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_coverage|4.1]]

I’m afraid the posts can’t tell us how Apple Photos performs, or why a specific search missed inside Google Photos.

*Would you like to see the actual phrases people typed first when hunting for a vaguely remembered photo?*

rows.question: How deep do people scroll through search results before deciding?
rows.restated: How far down in search results do people scroll before deciding (how deep do they go)?
withheld: unsupported number (a share in words does not fit): usually
unverifiable quote: how many results or minutes did you scroll?
rows.gap: few public posts say anything about how far down the results they went — 2 of 115 stories do — so it is left for interviews with real users
rows.draft:
**We can't tell how far people usually scroll — only two of the 115 cases say anything about that, one saying a few scrolls and one saying all the way down.** [[analysis_coverage|6.6]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:6.6=a_few_scrolls@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:6.6=exhaustive@photo_class:_all]]

Those two posts are the entire evidence in this evidence about scroll depth, so the public posts cannot settle a typical or median depth. [[analysis_coverage|6.6]][[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]] My read is that interviews are needed to measure this reliably because almost every other question about the search journey is likewise thinly reported here (for example, only 2 of 115 say how hurried they were and only 35 of 290 say why they picked a way of looking). [[analysis_coverage|1.4]][[analysis_coverage|3.3]][[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]]

What this does mean for work now is modest: we should not build product decisions assuming a common scroll limit from these posts. A likely reason is that people only mention scroll depth when it felt unusual or notable, so the public record over-represents extremes. Designing a follow-up interview study to ask "how many results or minutes did you scroll?" would answer the gap directly. [[analysis_coverage|6.6]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]]

*Want me to pull the two posts that mention scrolling so you can read their exact words?*
rows.text:
I'm sorry — my first draft made a claim the evidence doesn't fully support, so I've held it back rather than risk misleading you.

I'm afraid the evidence can't settle all of this: few public posts say anything about how far down the results they went — 2 of 115 cases do — so it is left for interviews with real users. [[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]]

The closest thing the evidence does show: In 2 of 7 cases about a photo the person only vaguely remembered, among posts on the Google Photos help forum, the first thing that went wrong was that they searched with what they remembered, but the photo wasn't in the results. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@source:gp_help]] In 2 of 11 cases about a photo the person only vaguely remembered, among posts on Hacker News, the first thing that went wrong was that they searched with what they remembered, but the photo wasn't in the results. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@source:hackernews]] In 5 of 8 cases about a photo the person only vaguely remembered, among posts on Reddit, the first thing that went wrong was that they searched with what they remembered, but the photo wasn't in the results. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@source:reddit]] [[story|e58ae2ef17027823d4aac979417e6bd78227e129:0]]

What people wrote about it: “scroll through google for hours” [[story|e58ae2ef17027823d4aac979417e6bd78227e129:0]] “after scrolling enough it was right there” [[story|1e8838fe6fe7c3028b1b5caf63177262024a2878:1]]

*Would you like me to go deeper into the cases where they searched with what they remembered, but the photo wasn't in the results?*

rows.question: How often does a wrong year act as a hard filter that hides the photo?
rows.restated: How often did people report that entering an incorrect year acted as a hard filter that hid the photo from results?
rows.gap: few public posts say anything about whether the system discarded the photo because one detail was wrong — 22 of 290 stories do — so it is left for interviews with real users
dropped: What this implies is modest — improving how searches cope with an incorrect year is worth testing in interviews because the public posts rarely report it and we cannot measure frequency from them.
rows.text:
**We can’t tell how often a wrong year acted as a hard filter; only 22 of the 290 cases say anything about whether one wrong detail caused the system to discard the photo, so the posts alone cannot settle that and interviews are needed.** [[analysis_coverage|5.3]][[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]]

That said, within the 115 cases about a vaguely remembered photo the few posts that mention a single-detail effect are split: in about a handful a small mistake did not matter, and in about a handful adding words made the photo disappear. [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:5.3=soft_ok@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:5.3=and_logic_shrinks_recall@photo_class:_all]] My read is that both patterns appear in the public posts but are rare there.

The posts cannot show whether search truly discarded images for a wrong year or whether people phrased queries poorly — that requires follow-up with users and controlled tests. [[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]][[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]]

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed when they described queries that made photos vanish?*

rows.question: How many attempts do people make before they give up?
rows.restated: How many attempts do people make before they give up trying to find a photo in Google Photos?
rows.gap: two AI readers went through the stories separately and agreed too rarely on how long they kept trying to rely on it
rows.text:
**30 of the 115 cases say how long the person kept trying; in those 30, 21 say they tried once, 6 say a few tries over minutes, and three say an hour or more.** [[analysis_coverage|8.1]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=one_attempt@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=few_attempts_minutes@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=hour_or_more@photo_class:_all]]

I'm afraid the posts can't settle this fully: the two AI readers agreed too rarely on “how long they kept trying,” so these numbers rest on the subset of cases that explicitly mention it and must be treated with caution. [[analysis_method_flags|low_reliability_fields]][[analysis_reliability|q:8.1]]

My read is that, among the cases that report it, the most common outcome is people trying once and stopping, which suggests short, single attempts are what shows up in public complaints; a likely reason is that people post when a quick try failed and they want help or to vent. This implies improving the first-search experience could help the largest group who report only one try. [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=one_attempt@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]]

*Want to see the actual phrases people used when describing their attempts?*

rows.question: Why does Ask Photos fail most often?
rows.restated: Why does Ask Photos fail most often?
dropped: The evidence shows that in the core set of 115 cases where people only vaguely remembered a photo, 31 cases began to fail at search results — the person searched with at least one correct detail, and the photo was not in the results they reported.
rows.text:
**Ask Photos most often fails because people type what they remember but the photo does not appear in the results — this was the first fault in about a quarter of the cases.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

The next largest single first failure was photos already gone (about one in six cases). [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

My read is that fixing how short, imperfect queries are matched would reach the largest group: if search returned the photo when someone supplied one right detail, fewer hunts would stop there. A likely reason this step dominates is that people often have just a single remembered cue (time, object, person), so failures at the results block the whole journey. This suggests prioritising better handling of short, partly-correct queries and surfacing near-misses. The posts can't settle why search missed each query internally, so we cannot say whether the fault was indexing, ranking, or query phrasing. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_reliability|primary_stage]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]]

*Want to see what people actually typed when the search step failed?*

rows.question: Since most failures happen because the photo was deleted, what should Google fix first?
rows.restated: Since most failures happen because the photo was deleted, what should Google fix first?
rows.text:
**Not so—the posts cannot show that most failures are because the photo was deleted; for vaguely remembered photos the single biggest fixable problem found is that search did not return the photo when people typed what they remembered, which is the first failure in about a quarter of cases.** [[analysis_opportunity|stage0]][[analysis_opportunity|stage5]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]

In the 115 cases about a vaguely remembered photo, the first thing that went wrong was search failing to return the photo in 31 cases (the largest ranked group), while the photo already gone appears first in 20 cases (about one in six). [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:_all]]

My read is that improving how Photos interprets short, underspecified cues would help most: the posts report single‑word queries and irrelevant, overbroad or empty results, and the study recommends testing AI to expand/disambiguate simple cues and make query logic more tolerant. [[analysis_synthesis|recommendation:chain:evidence]][[analysis_synthesis|recommendation:root_cause]][[analysis_synthesis|recommendation:intelligence_needed]]

The posts cannot reveal why search missed at an internal level or how fixes will perform in real users; interviews are needed to validate which cue‑expansions and refinements actually surface targets. [[analysis_opportunity|stage5]][[analysis_synthesis|recommendation:top]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]][[analysis_synthesis|recommendation:label]]

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed first?*

rows.question: What share of utility-photo stories end with the person giving up?
rows.restated: What share of practical-photo stories end with the person giving up?
rows.gap: only 21 stories are about photos kept for the information in them (receipts, documents, notes) — too few (under 30) for a percentage, so only counts are given
rows.text:
**I can't give a reliable share because there are only 21 utility-photo cases, so I can only report counts: 8 of those 21 ended because the photo was already gone and 6 of the 21 say they found it.** [[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]]

What the posts show for utility photos (receipts, documents, notes) is therefore this small-count picture: 8 people first discovered the photo was deleted or never backed up, 6 found the photo, 4 couldn't remember enough to search, and 3 tried searching but the photo did not appear in results. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]]

My read is that deletion/loss is the single largest named reason among these 21 cases, so fixing backup/sync or surfacing offline copies would help those people most. That said, treat this as a hint: with only 21 cases we cannot generalise to a percentage of all such attempts. [[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]]

*Want the exact phrases people used when searching for receipts and documents?*

rows.question: What share of stories about photos kept for both sentimental and practical reasons fail at search?
rows.restated: What proportion of stories about photos that were kept for both sentimental and practical reasons describe a failure at search (i.e., finding the photo went wrong at some step rather than “nothing went wrong”)?
rows.gap: no stories bear on this in detail; none of the stories is about photos kept both as memories and for the information in them, so nothing can be said about them
rows.text:
**I’m afraid the posts can’t settle that: none of the cases is about photos kept both for sentimental and for practical reasons, so the study has no evidence to give a share for that group.** [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]]

That said, here is what the study does show about nearby groups you might care about. For photos kept as memories (people, trips, events), roughly a third of cases found the photo without anything going wrong, and roughly a quarter first failed because the person searched with what they remembered but the photo wasn’t in the results — a small group, so treat these as rough guides. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:sentimental]] For photos kept for their information (receipts, documents, notes), the most common first problem was that the photo was already gone. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]]

My read is that if you want to know the split for photos kept both for memory and information, we need cases that explicitly say that motive; the public posts here don’t include them. [[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]][[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]]

*Want me to pull the exact posts that show what people typed when search failed for memory photos?*

rows.question: How many core stories are there, and from how many different people?
rows.restated: How many stories about a vaguely remembered photo are in the stories, and how many distinct people authored them?
rows.text:
**There are 115 core cases, told by 109 different people.** [[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

That 115 is the set the study treats as the half‑remembered, or core, cases; the posts in that set were written by 109 distinct people. [[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

I'm afraid the posts can't tell us anything beyond those counts — they don't represent all users or searches, and public posts over‑represent problems. [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]]

*Want to see the posts behind those 115 cases?*

rows.question: How many core stories first go wrong because search did not understand or match what was typed?
rows.restated: How many stories about a vaguely remembered photo first go wrong because search did not understand or match what was typed?
rows.text:
**In 31 of the 115 core cases (the most common single first failure), the first thing that went wrong was that they searched with what they remembered but the photo wasn't in the results.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

That figure comes directly from the cases about photos people only vaguely remembered: 31 cases were marked where the person typed what they recalled and the photo did not appear. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]] My read is that this points to a substantial group whose remembered detail was concrete enough to try, yet the query did not return the target — whether because of wording, indexing, or other reasons we cannot see from posts. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_reliability|primary_stage]]

This suggests prioritising improvements that help when a short, specific query fails: better handling of brief queries, clearer feedback when nothing matches, and easier ways to reformulate a search. A likely reason is that people expect a one-shot text query to find a half-remembered photo, so helping that moment will help the largest group. (I'm afraid the posts cannot settle why search missed in each case.) [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_reliability|primary_stage]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]]

*Want to see examples of what people actually typed when that happened?*

rows.question: And how does that split by kind of photo?
rows.restated: Which step of the finding the photo journey is most often the first place things go wrong, and how does that distribution differ by kind of photo (sentimental, practical, both, unclear)?
withheld: comparison between kinds of photo: differs by kind of photo
rows.draft:
**You can’t reliably say the first break differs by kind of photo because the groups are too small to compare; here’s the split for each kind on its own.** [[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]

Among photos kept as memories (people, trips, events): nothing went wrong in about a third of cases, and the first thing that went wrong most often was that people searched with what they remembered but the photo wasn't in the results — about a quarter of these cases. Deleted/never-backed-up photos and not using the search box each account for about one in eight cases; spotting the photo among similar ones, not remembering enough, and posts that only say why they were looking are all only a handful of cases. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=1@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:sentimental]]

Among photos whose post does not say why they were kept: about a third found the photo, about a third first failed because their query didn’t return the photo, and deletions and hard-to-spot results each account for about one in eight; a few never used the search box or couldn’t remember enough. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:unclear]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:unclear]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:unclear]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:unclear]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:unclear]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:unclear]]

Among photos kept for information (receipts, documents, notes): counts only — the most common first break was that the photo was already gone (8 of 21); finding the photo occurred in 6 of 21, failing to remember enough in 4 of 21, and query-without-result in 3 of 21. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]]

My read is that improving how short, vague queries match candidate photos would help across all three groups because “query returned no target” appears in each.

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed when the search returned the wrong results?*

I'm sorry — my first draft made a claim the evidence doesn't fully support, so I've held it back rather than risk misleading you.

The closest thing the evidence does show: In 13 of 48 cases (27%) about a photo the person only vaguely remembered, among photos kept as memories (people, trips, events), the first thing that went wrong was that they searched with what they remembered, but the photo wasn't in the results — a small group, so only a rough guide. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:sentimental]] In 15 of 46 cases (33%) about a photo the person only vaguely remembered, among photos whose post does not say why they were kept, the first thing that went wrong was that they searched with what they remembered, but the photo wasn't in the results — a small group, so only a rough guide. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:unclear]] In 3 of 21 cases about a photo the person only vaguely remembered, among photos kept for the information in them (receipts, documents, notes), the first thing that went wrong was that they searched with what they remembered, but the photo wasn't in the results. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]] [[story|cbc995976ab0e7519ef70d4d3bf1b20c0485baf8:0]]

What people wrote about it: “but instead my phone only shows photos of Boba Fett” [[story|cbc995976ab0e7519ef70d4d3bf1b20c0485baf8:0]] “it found photos of my cats instead of me with beard journey” [[story|3ba2ad97300ec1206044dc3deed79e0240a13297:1]] “it returned way too many images of my shop” [[story|0ef3821f2d59998617a4b53f428fd49c9a22d2ff:0]]

rows.question: Does that differ for utility photos?
rows.restated: Do people who look for practical photos (e.g., receipts, bills, product photos) tend to type different first-search queries compared with the overall set (i.e., is the single-word-first pattern different for practical photos)?
rows.gap: only 21 stories are about photos kept for the information in them (receipts, documents, notes) — too few (under 30) for a percentage, so only counts are given
rows.text:
**I’m afraid the groups are too small to compare reliably — there are only 21 cases about utility photos, so I can only report counts, not a typical pattern.** [[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=several_keywords@photo_class:utility]]

Of those 21 utility-photo cases, 3 say the person typed a single word first (for example “passport”), and 2 say they typed several keywords (for example “driver's license” in the post). [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=several_keywords@photo_class:utility]][[story|765749899f7fa8a7f4c8527cc2337029e134b9ce:0]][[story|4bc6fae93ac441d7708072e0871976ae3562b9a6:0]]

My read is that when people keep photos for information they still sometimes try a single strong cue (a document name) but also sometimes use multiple keywords; that suggests testing both short noun queries and short phrase queries in interviews to see which users prefer and which the product must handle better. This evidence cannot tell us whether utility photos behave differently from memory photos because the utility group is too small to compare. [[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:sentimental]]

rows.draft:
**The full journey usually runs from “photo there?” to “gave up or found it”, and the single biggest problem was that search returned no matching result first — about a quarter of the cases failed that way.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]

We read each case along the path: was the photo present, why they wanted it, what they remembered and forgot, where they looked (search box or scrolling), how they put the memory into words, whether those words produced results, whether they could spot the photo among results, whether they tried again, and how it ended. [[analysis_funnel|stories:core]] Two AI readers agreed on where the first failure was in most cases, showing consistent reading though not proof of correctness. [[analysis_reliability|primary_stage]][[analysis_method_flags|no_gold_standard]]

In roughly one third the person found the photo at once. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]] In about a quarter the first failure was that the person searched with what they remembered but the photo wasn’t in the results. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]] Other first failures were the photo already gone (about one in six), never using the search box (about one in ten), the photo being hard to spot among similar results (about one in ten), or the person not remembering enough to search (about one in twenty). [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:_all]]

My read is that improving how short, vague queries are handled would reach the largest group: better matching of brief remembered words to photos would convert many of the cases marked as “search returned nothing.” This suggests prioritising clearer feedback for no-result queries and smarter ranking of likely matches. A likely reason some searches failed is that people gave one correct detail and another wrong or omitted one, so the query scope missed the target. Note I can’t see why a search missed from the posts themselves, only that people say it did. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]]

dropped: Taken together, these cases show people typically try concise, often object or label-style words first when a photo is only vaguely remembered.
rows.text:
**People often started with a single word: about a quarter of the cases that say what they typed begin with one word.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_coverage|4.1]]

Three-word-exact phrases from the posts, with context:
- the post says “searched ‘forest’ in my gallery” — looking for old fall photos, and a single word search returned results. [[story|346adeec584d4ac2df9090145e995deb4acb616e:0]] - the post says “search Google Photos for “bicycle”” — couldn’t remember the date, so they typed the object word. [[story|790de55c9d650cb50647f97841544a0c5b1b7275:0]] - the post says “I just search for “passport”” — kept documents and found them by that single word. [[story|4bc6fae93ac441d7708072e0871976ae3562b9a6:0]] - the post says “searching for tatoo” — trying to find an old photo of a tattoo by that word. [[story|aa1520f4fbb8f25b2e1435cc95c2f9fd8d6616fe:0]] - the post says “test a bunch of search words” — they tried several single-word queries and got no luck. [[story|4f97934e36516780fd57de1c6d42d5da089277a5:0]]

My read is that improving how short, single-word queries are handled would likely help many of these searches. [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_coverage|4.1]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=several_keywords@photo_class:_all]]

**People looking for a receipt most often report typing the item name and getting nothing — for example:** "I couldn't find the receipt for my laptop, 'receipt' returned nothing" (looking for a receipt; the post says it returned nothing) [[story|probe-inj-04]]; "I search google photos for 'Boba'…instead my phone only shows photos of Boba Fett" (looking for a shop/receipt or place; irrelevant matches shown) [[story|cbc995976ab0e7519ef70d4d3bf1b20c0485baf8:0]]; "I was looking for a scrap receipt and had Google photos look up 'scrap' and it returned way too many images of my shop" (looking for a receipt; too many unrelated results) [[story|0ef3821f2d59998617a4b53f428fd49c9a22d2ff:0]].

rows.question: What happens when people search for a pet photo and cannot find it?
rows.restated: What happens when people search for a pet photo and cannot find it?
rows.text:
**When people hunt for a vaguely remembered pet photo, about a quarter first fail because they searched with what they remembered but the photo didn’t appear in the results.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

Three brief phrases from the posts, with context:
- the person looked for a dog at the park but “'dog park' never finds the photo of my dog at the park in winter” (the post says). [[story|probe-inj-06]]
- someone tried “I can put in 'dog' and see that it's listing too many photos” (the post says), so results were noisy. [[story|c06874c9c9acadf8038072c41b2d0d2c08c2bc10:0]]
- another reports searching “dog on beach” and not finding a beloved picture they knew existed (the post says). [[story|c06874c9c9acadf8038072c41b2d0d2c08c2bc10:0]]

Taken together these show a pattern: people often remember a single pet detail and try it, yet the search results either omit the target or return too many similar images, so the photo isn’t spotted. My read is that improving how short, single-word or short-phrase pet queries are interpreted would help the largest group who go looking with a half-memory. [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:_all]]
